description: I'm Sushil Muthuvelkumar, a freshman mechanical engineering student at NJIT. I'm building an AI-powered dashboard to explore microgravity combustion data and improve fire safety for space exploration. My background is in CAD (Onshape/SolidWorks), robotics (FTC), and coding. I'm starting solo and welcome teammates interested in data, AI, and space.
summary: Decades of microgravity fire experiments are hard to find, compare and trust. Flamefall Analytics is a web console that summarises, ranks and interprets them for people designing crewed spacecraft, stations, lunar bases and pressurised rovers. It holds to three rules: every number carries its source down to the table and test number; where nobody ran the test it says "no data" and shows the nearest real tests; and it gives estimates with their uncertainty, never a verdict. Its core is 276 droplet-burn tests, 313 solid-material test points and 66 sourced statements. The two datasets were checked against their primary sources cell by cell and row by row; of the 66 statements, 60 were verified against the source they cite, and the six that could not be are shown greyed with the reason. Checking changed fourteen statements in our own research notes, and the console shows where its own model fails. Sushil Muthuvelkumar (team owner) chose the challenge, set the research questions, made the product and design decisions, directed the build and verified the final numbers; Claude Code implemented the console and deck, and an AI research assistant compiled the source material.
details:
Who did what. Sushil Muthuvelkumar (team owner, NJIT freshman) chose the Flame in Freefall challenge, registered the team and moved it to the Universal virtual event; set the research direction and depth, including three rounds of checking against the primary NASA documents; made the product decisions — a 7-slide deck instead of a video, the Next.js / shadcn / Recharts stack, and the design rules; directed the build through detailed briefs; and verified the live console and deck himself. Srikar Mattegunta joined as the second member for eligibility. Claude Code (Fable 5.2) wrote the code, data pipeline, console and slide deck as directed, and an AI research assistant compiled the research notes and analysed the FLEX droplet data.

What it does. Six pages. FLEX Explorer: all 276 droplet burns, filterable by fuel, oxygen, pressure, diluent and outcome, with extinction share by gas level, burning rate, and a per-row source. Investigation Catalogue: every combustion investigation the repository returns, with objective, materials, conditions, key finding and record link; a search that answers with the measured statements themselves; and ranking against a scenario by a stated rule. Scenario Lab: set oxygen, pressure, ventilation flow, material and gravity; get the nearest real tests, a model estimate where a validated model exists, and an explicit "no data" panel otherwise. Model Lab: grouped cross-validation results, confusion matrices, calibration, what moved the prediction, and a distance-to-data warning. What We Don't Know: partial gravity, solids above the tested oxygen range, CO2 with helium, and three kinds of burning a crew cannot see. Overview: the headline numbers.

What we found by going back to the sources. In 39 of the 60 n-heptane tests logged as "Extinction", the report's own captions describe evidence that the droplet kept burning as a cool flame after the visible flame was gone. "No visible flame" is not "fire out". Methanol droplets went out in 80.3% of tests and n-heptane in 50.4% in the same apparatus: fuel chemistry matters as much as atmosphere. The solid-material memo that our notes listed as unobtainable is on NTRS under its real file name. We transcribed 126 tests from it and checked every row against the page. "85% oxygen" in the repository is the burner feed of inside-out flames, not a cabin atmosphere. Chamber oxygen never exceeded 40%. No lunar- or Martian-gravity combustion dataset is in the repository. The nearest real evidence is one suborbital flight's preliminary slides, shown with that label. A model for solid materials, built exactly as specified, does no better than chance on test series it has not seen (AUC 0.48). We report that and do not use it.

How SI is used inside the console. Retrieval and extraction over sourced statements (no generated text), ranking by a written formula with adjustable weights, and small logistic models tested on groups of tests they never saw: AUC 0.88 on unseen atmospheres and 0.74 on an unseen fuel for droplet extinction.

Benefits. A reviewer can click from any number to its table. A designer can see at once whether a planned atmosphere was ever tested. A student can see how a model is validated honestly, including one that fails.

Tools. Next.js (React, App Router), shadcn/ui, Recharts, Motion, react-countup, the Sera UI liquid-glass surface, TypeScript and Vitest for the web app, hosted on Render as a static site; Python, pandas, scikit-learn and pytest for the data and models, run at build time only.

NASA data and resources used and linked: PSI Data Repository, combustion science: https://psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion (26 records and 25 experimental tables). NASA Combustion Science: https://www.nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science/ Found by the team, not provided on the challenge's Resources tab: Dietrich et al., NASA/TP-2015-216046 (FLEX): https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20150023456 ; Olson et al., NASA/TM-20210011385 (BASS-II): https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20210011385 ; Urban et al., ICES-2024-365 and ICES-2026-577 (Saffire): https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240002981 , https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20260001992 ; Urban et al., AIAA 2012-3536 (SAME-R): https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20130000422 ; Ferkul et al., ASGSR 2025 (LUCI): https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20250010653

Space agency partner and other data: Urban et al., SAME Final Report (NIST): https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=904707 . Further papers are cited per statement in data/evidence.json in the repository.

Use of SI (short disclosure): SI tools were used throughout and are disclosed in full in the repository (docs/SI_DISCLOSURE.md). Research notes: an SI research assistant compiled the initial research notes from public sources before the build. Code, data pipeline, web console and slide deck: written with Claude Code (Anthropic, model Claude Fable 5.2) acting as an SI coding agent, directed by the team. Code review: Loopy, an SI code-review bot, reviewed the first four pull requests; it stopped on 14 Nov when the organisation's monthly review allowance ran out, before any pull request reached its top score. After that the pull requests were self-reviewed by the SI coding agent in passes. Inside the console there is no generative model. "SI-powered" means three auditable things: retrieval and extraction over sourced statements (TF-IDF search, no generated text), ranking by a stated formula with visible weights, and small logistic-regression models validated by grouped cross-validation. The console cannot produce a number that is not in a data file. No SI-generated images, video or audio are used. Charts are drawn from the data by code. Verification: the SI coding agent checked numbers against primary sources with scripts anyone can re-run: the core dataset cell by cell with two independent parsers; the solid-fuel tables row by row against the page text; literature values against the cited table or page. Not every number is verified. Two statements rest on an abstract only and four could not be re-read; each is marked as such where it is shown.
